title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 14: Engendering the Judiciary
keywords: Strategic Gender and Development Mainstreaming Plan
Committee on Gender Responsiveness in the Judiciary
Rule on Violence Against Women and Their Children

Guidelines on Proper Work Decorum in the Judiciary

primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's Women's Month address on how far and how fast women have reshaped the Philippine legal profession and judiciary, and on what the Supreme Court has done to make itself gender-responsive.

A statistical account of women's advance: more than half the graduating classes of three leading law colleges, a rise from 3.5 percent of bar passers before World War II to 40.6 percent in 1996-2005, and the present count of female justices and judges at every level of the courts.

The Court's gender program -- the Strategic Gender and Development Mainstreaming Plan, the Committee on Gender Responsiveness in the Judiciary (the first of its kind in Asia), the rules on violence against women and on harassment, the work-decorum guidelines, and the new Manual of Judicial Writing -- together with CJP's own long practice of rewriting decisions to avoid gender-biased pronouns.

The enlistment of women judges in his reform agenda -- the four Ins, the plague of 'ships,' and the ACID problems -- held up against three exemplars, Justices Cecilia Muñoz-Palma, Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera and Carolina C. Griño-Aquino.
sub_topics: The occasion: Women's Month, and the Court's exhibit of March 8 honoring its female justices under the theme 'Gender-Responsive Philippine Judiciary: KKK (Kamalayan, Katarungan, Kababaihan),' whose success makes CJP concede that women are better event organizers than men.

Women's entry into a once predominantly male enclave: for the last five years more than 50 percent of the graduating classes of three leading law colleges have been female, prompting old professors to joke that male law students may become an endangered species.

Bar statistics: only 287 women against 7,846 men admitted from 1901 to 1945, but 4,430 women against 6,493 men in 1996-2005 -- from 3.5 percent to 40.6 percent of passers, with women likely to outnumber men soon.
A Supreme Court study with UNDP and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation showing a higher percentage of female lawyers in the academe and in NGOs.

The female factor on the bench: five of fifteen justices of the Supreme Court, 17 of 62 in the Court of Appeals, 3 of 14 in a Sandiganbayan headed by a woman presiding justice, two of six in the Court of Tax Appeals, and 419 female against 1,075 male lower-court judges.

The Strategic Gender and Development Mainstreaming Plan, formulated by the Committee on Gender Responsiveness in the Judiciary -- the first such committee in Asia -- aimed at gender-responsive judges, lawyers, personnel, rules, procedures and facilities.

The issuances that stress gender equality: the Rule on Violence Against Women and Their Children, the Rule on Administrative Procedure in Harassment Cases, the Guidelines on Proper Work Decorum in the Judiciary, the New Code of Judicial Conduct and the Code of Conduct for Court Personnel; plus a proposed audit of all rules and issuances for gender-insensitive language.
The new Manual of Judicial Writing, downloadable from the Supreme Court website, which encourages gender-sensitive language in decisions and resolutions.

The evidence that English and Philippine legal texts carry a male bias: the Bill of Rights on the accused and on self-incrimination, the constitutional qualifications for Senator, President and member of the Supreme Court, Article 1305 of the Civil Code on contracts, and Rule 126 of the Rules of Court on arraignment.
The convenient excuse he rejects -- the canon of construction that the masculine, but not the feminine, includes all genders unless the context indicates otherwise.

CJP's own techniques, used long before the Manual appeared: pluralizing the accused, recasting sentences to drop the pronoun, and rephrasing constitutional qualifications as 'The President' or 'A senator' shall be 'a natural-born citizen.'

His reform pledge on assuming office on December 21, 2005 -- the four Ins, a judiciary morally courageous against influence, interference, insolence and indifference, judges impervious to the plague of 'ships,' and the battle against the ACID problems, all aimed at safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

The call for women judges to contribute in cerebral and ethical terms rather than by numbers alone, with Justice Cecilia Muñoz-Palma as the model of independence, integrity, industry and intelligence, Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera as PhilJA's indefatigable chancellor, and Justice Carolina C. Griño-Aquino as MCLE chairperson.
The closing charge: those who serve in the judiciary have taken the less traveled road toward the judicial renaissance he hopes for.

stances.claim: Women's advance in Philippine law is real and measurable, and on present trends female bar passers will soon outnumber males.
stances.rhetorical_move: statistical demonstration: enrollment figures, bar-admission counts across two eras, and court-by-court headcounts marshalled before any argument is made

stances.claim: Legal language carries a pronounced male bias that judges should not simply reproduce; the rule of construction that the masculine includes all genders is a 'convenient excuse' rather than a justification.
stances.rhetorical_move: example-then-technique: quoting the Constitution, the Civil Code and the Rules of Court to prove the bias, then showing his own pluralizing and sentence-recasting fixes

stances.claim: Women judges are meant to contribute far more than numbers: it is the philosophies, values and inspiration they bring that should make the difference in a reformed judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: raising the ask: converting a celebratory occasion into recruitment for his reform agenda, with named exemplars as the standard

stances.claim: Justice Cecilia Muñoz-Palma exemplified independence, integrity, industry and intelligence -- independence above all when she faced up to a dictator who was her own appointing authority.
stances.rhetorical_move: biographical proof of the four Ins: mapping each 'In' onto an episode of one magistrate's life so the standard becomes concrete and imitable

notable_anecdotes: CJP concedes, after the success of the March 8 exhibit honoring the Court's female justices, that women are better and more effective event organizers than men.
He repeats the apprehension of some old-time professors that with more than half of law graduates now female, male law students may become an endangered species in the next 10 or 20 years.

He shows his own drafting practice, rewriting 'reading to the accused the charges leveled against him' as 'against them,' and recasting a line on a convicted lawyer to drop the masculine pronoun entirely.

He recalls Justice Cecilia Muñoz-Palma standing up for her principles against the dictator who had appointed her, praises Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera's 'indomitable spirit, sharp intellect and tireless passion for work' at PhilJA, and notes that Justice Carolina C. Griño-Aquino topped the 1950 bar, practiced for 20 years, and had 42 happy years of marriage with the late Chief Justice Ramon C. Aquino.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's Women's Month address, delivered days after the Court's March 8 exhibit honoring its female justices under the theme 'Gender-Responsive Philippine Judiciary: KKK (Kamalayan, Katarungan, Kababaihan).' He traced how quickly women had reshaped a once predominantly male profession: more than half the graduating classes of three leading law colleges over five years were female, prompting old professors to joke that male law students might become an endangered species; only 287 women against 7,846 men were admitted to the bar from 1901 to 1945, but 4,430 women against 6,493 men passed between 1996 and 2005, lifting the female share from 3.5 percent to 40.6 percent. He gave the counts on the bench -- five of fifteen Supreme Court justices, 17 in the Court of Appeals, three in a Sandiganbayan led by a woman presiding justice, two in the Court of Tax Appeals, and 419 lower-court judges -- and cited a Court study with UNDP and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation showing more female lawyers in academe and NGOs. He described the Court's Strategic Gender and Development Mainstreaming Plan, its Committee on Gender Responsiveness (the first in Asia), the rules on violence against women and on harassment, the work-decorum guidelines, the codes of conduct, a proposed audit of issuances for gender-insensitive language, and the new Manual of Judicial Writing. Observing that the English language is not gender-friendly, he quoted masculine pronouns in the Bill of Rights, the qualifications for Senator, President and Supreme Court member, Article 1305 of the Civil Code and Rule 126 on arraignment, rejected the 'convenient excuse' that the masculine includes all genders, and showed how he had long pluralized or recast his own sentences to avoid sexist language. He then enlisted women judges in his agenda of the four Ins, the plague of 'ships' and the ACID problems, holding up Justices Cecilia Muñoz-Palma, Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera and Carolina C. Griño-Aquino as models, and closed by praising those who had taken the less traveled road toward a judicial renaissance.
